Plato's dialogues keep returning to a few questions: what is real, how we can know it, how we should live, and how a political community should be organized. This section follows those questions through fifteen chapters.

Each chapter starts from a question, distinguishes what the characters of the dialogues argue from what can cautiously be attributed to Plato, and points to the passages where you can read the arguments yourself.

## I. Reality and Knowledge

What is real, and how can we know it?

- [Theory of Forms](/resources/philosophy/theory-of-forms.html) — Why several dialogues distinguish changing sensible things from stable, intelligible realities, and the objections Plato himself raises.
- [The Allegory of the Cave](/resources/philosophy/the-cave-allegory.html) — Prisoners, shadows and a difficult turn toward the light: an image of education and its risks.
- [The Divided Line](/resources/philosophy/the-divided-line.html) — Four ways of grasping things, from images to understanding, and where mathematical thinking fits.
- [Appearance and Reality](/resources/philosophy/appearance-vs-reality.html) — When can appearances be trusted, and when must they be examined? Being and becoming.
- [Knowledge and Opinion](/resources/philosophy/knowledge-vs-opinion.html) — Is a true opinion enough? What knowledge adds, from the *Meno* to the *Theaetetus*.
- [Recollection and Learning](/resources/philosophy/recollection-learning.html) — How can we search for what we do not know? Meno's challenge and the idea that learning is recollection.

## II. The Soul, Virtue and Love

How should we live, and what moves us?

- [The Soul](/resources/philosophy/the-soul.html) — Inner conflict, the winged chariot of the *Phaedrus* and the arguments about immortality.
- [Virtue and the Good Life](/resources/philosophy/virtue-ethics.html) — Can virtue be taught? Are the virtues one? Justice and happiness.
- [The Form of the Good](/resources/philosophy/the-good.html) — The image of the sun and why the Good is presented as the most important object of study.
- [Beauty and Love](/resources/philosophy/beauty-and-love.html) — The many voices of the *Symposium*, the ascent toward Beauty and the *Phaedrus*.

## III. The City, Education and Art

Who should govern, and how should citizens be formed?

- [The Just City](/resources/philosophy/ideal-state.html) — The city built in speech: tasks, virtues, the myth of the metals and the objections it invites.
- [Plato's Critique of Democracy](/resources/philosophy/democracy-critique.html) — Freedom, the democratic person and how tyranny could emerge, read against the Athens of Plato's time.
- [Philosopher-Rulers: Knowledge and the Burden of Power](/resources/philosophy/philosopher-kings.html) — Why philosophers should govern, and why they would rather not.
- [Education: Learning to Turn Around](/resources/philosophy/education-theory.html) — Education as a change in the direction of attention, from music and physical training to dialectic.
- [Art and Poetry: Images, Knowledge and Emotion](/resources/philosophy/art-poetry.html) — The challenge to the poets in the *Republic*, and inspiration in the *Ion* and the *Phaedrus*.
